summary: Defines a framework and requirements for a mechanism by which a network access server controls an access node, such as a DSLAM, in broadband multi-service networks. It allows direct device-to-device communication for service, quality of service and subscriber operations. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally a broadband provider's central server and the cabinet in the street are coordinated through management systems, which are slow and often belong to different departments. This RFC proposes a direct link between the two, so that things like the real speed of a line or a change to a video channel can be handled straight away.

questions: what is an access node control mechanism
what are multicast white and grey lists
subtitle: A direct link between a provider's central server and the cabinet in the street, for the things that cannot wait for the management systems.

tldr.problem: The central server and the street cabinet that serve a broadband line are coordinated through management systems, which are slow, do not cross organisational boundaries well, and were not built to pass control data in real time.
tldr.mechanism: The Access Node Control Mechanism lets the server and the cabinet talk directly, with a controller function on the server side and reporting and enforcement functions on the cabinet side.
tldr.outcome: It defines no protocol but gives a framework, four use cases, and 124 numbered requirements for the protocol and for the two kinds of network element.

facts.label: Access Nodes one NAS must control

today: RFC 5851 is an Informational document published in May 2010, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a framework and a requirements document: it defines no protocol, but it describes the use cases for direct communication between a network access server and an access node and lists the numbered requirements from R-1 to R-124, with the security requirements handed over to RFC 5713.

sections.title: Why a Direct Link Between Server and Cabinet
sections.content:
DSL is widely deployed for broadband access. Several Broadband Forum documents describe possible architectures for these access networks, covering the delivery of voice, video and data services. The framework here is aimed at DSL access, whether ATM/DSL or Ethernet/DSL, and is meant to stay open to other access technologies such as passive optical networks or wireless, although the details are out of scope.

Traditional architectures need a permanent virtual circuit per subscriber, configured at layer 2 and terminated at the first layer 3 device such as a Broadband Remote Access Server. Alongside the data plane, they define architectures for element, network and service management. Interworking at the management plane is not always possible, because of the organisational boundaries between the departments operating the local loop, the ATM network and the IP network, and because management networks are usually not designed to pass management data between those entities in real time.

Value-added services across DSL access need close attention to quality of service and service control, which means tighter coordination between the network nodes, the access nodes and the network access server, without burdening the Operational Support Systems with impractical expectations.

That is what the Access Node Control Mechanism is for: a way for the network access server and the access node to exchange service, quality-of-service and subscriber information directly, without the information having to pass through separate element managers. Access-link operations can then happen inside those network elements while the existing operational support systems are left alone. The RFC gives a framework for such a mechanism, identifies the use cases that justify it, and then presents the requirements for the protocol that would carry it and for the network elements that support it. The requirements are based on work done by the Broadband Forum.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the provider's central server and the cabinet in the street are coordinated through the management systems, which are slow and often sit in different departments. This RFC proposes a direct link between the two, for the things that need to happen quickly.

sections.title: The Architecture and the Three Functions
sections.content:
The reference architecture can be built on ATM or on Ethernet access and aggregation. For a legacy ATM aggregation network introducing quality-of-service-enabled IP services, it builds on Broadband Forum TR-059; for an Ethernet aggregation network supporting new IP services including Ethernet multicast replication, it builds on TR-101. Given the industry's move towards Ethernet, the primary focus is on the TR-101 architecture, but the concepts apply equally to an ATM one.

The pieces are: the home gateway, which connects the customer premises equipment to the access node and the access network and is, for DSL, a network termination device that may act as a layer 2 bridge or a layer 3 router; the access loop, which gives physical connectivity between the home gateway and the access node and may group several DSL links together into one virtual link by DSL bonding; the access node, which may support several access-loop technologies, terminates them, and can also aggregate traffic from other access nodes; the access node uplink, which must provide traffic aggregation, class of service distinction, and customer separation and traceability; the aggregation network, which aggregates traffic towards the NAS; the network access server, which interfaces to the aggregation network and to the regional network and plays the central role in per-subscriber policy enforcement and quality of service; and the regional network, which connects NASes and access networks to network and application service providers.

Three functions make up the mechanism. The controller function sends requests for information, or triggers behaviour in the element where the reporting or enforcement function lives. The reporting function conveys status information to the controller, for example the access-loop data rate from an access node to a network access server that is shaping traffic to that rate. The enforcement function is contacted by the controller to trigger a remote action on the access node, for example starting a port test or deciding whether a multicast join is honoured or denied.

The message flow is that the access node sends an information report or an admission request towards the NAS, the NAS answers with an admission response or a control request, and the access node closes with a control response. How often those messages are generated depends on the use case. The use cases are described abstractly, independent of any protocol mapping, and the actual protocol specification is out of scope, but certain characteristics of the protocol are required so that specification, implementation, debugging and troubleshooting are simpler and so that more use cases can be added later.
sections.plainLanguage: The mechanism has three parts: something that asks for information, something that reports what it knows, and something that carries out an instruction. The cabinet reports the line's real speed, the server asks for changes, and the cabinet carries them out.

sections.title: The Use Cases
sections.content:
Access topology discovery. A NAS that applies hierarchical scheduling needs to know the topology of the access network, the links being used and their rates. Some of that information is dynamic, such as the DSL line rate and therefore the net data rate, so it cannot come from a provisioning or inventory management system; some changes less often, such as the capacity of a DSLAM uplink, but still has to be kept strictly in step between the actual capacity and the image the server holds. Operational support systems are not typically designed to enforce that consistency reliably and scalably across organisational boundaries, so this use case lets the NAS get the information without integrating with an operational support system.

Communicating access-loop attributes matters especially when the rate changes over time. The actual data rate may differ every time the network termination device is turned on, in which case the access node sends an information report after the line resynchronises. While the line is active the rate can also change, because the loop can fall out of sync and retrain to a lower value, or because seamless rate adaptation makes the rate fluctuate; then the access node sends an additional information report each time the attributes change above a threshold. What the NAS needs is the identification and speed of the access loop and of the remote terminal or access node uplink. Beyond that, the access node can report a long list of loop characteristics: the DSL type, the framing mode, the port state, the actual and maximum achievable net data rates, the minimum and maximum configured net data rates, the minimum net data rate in low power state, and the maximum achievable and actual interleaving delays.

Access-loop configuration. Access-loop rates are typically configured statically, so a subscriber who wants a different rate forces the operator to reconfigure the access port, which may mean a business-to-business transaction between an internet service provider and an access provider. That is costly in operating expenditure. Doing it from the NAS through the mechanism avoids those cross-organisation interactions and lets subscriber service data be centralised in a policy server. The best way to change parameters is by using profiles, pre-configured on the access nodes by the element manager, with the NAS sending a reference to the right profile in a configure request. The same mechanism can carry parameters that are not specific to the access-loop technology, such as the quality-of-service profile for a loop, or the per-subscriber multicast entitlement used for IPTV where the access node is doing IGMP snooping or proxying. If the adjacency with the access node is down, the NAS cannot make the change and should report the failure to the external management system.

Remote connectivity test. Traditionally, ATM circuits are point-to-point between the server and the cabinet or the network termination device, and layer 2 connectivity is tested with operations, administration and maintenance functionality: an end-to-end loopback between the edge devices. When the aggregation network moves to Ethernet, end-to-end ATM OAM no longer applies, and end-to-end Ethernet OAM would be the ideal answer, but most home gateways did not support those procedures, and each access technology has its own link-based mechanisms. Triggered by a local management interface, the NAS can use the mechanism to start an access-loop test between the access node and the home gateway. On an ATM access loop the access node can be told to generate F4 or F5 loopback cells; on Ethernet it can perform a port synchronisation and administrative test. The result comes back to the NAS in a control response and can be passed on through a local management interface, so the connectivity between the server and the home gateway can be monitored by a single trigger event.

Multicast. In an ATM access network, multicast replication happens in the NAS, which terminates and processes the subscriber IGMP messages, while the access nodes and aggregation switches do neither, so network resources are wasted in the access network. Involving the access node, the aggregation nodes and the NAS in the replication avoids several copies of the same stream crossing the access network; on Ethernet this can be done with IGMP snooping or proxying in the access node and aggregation nodes. For backward compatibility with the ATM model, the three then have to behave as a single logical device with the same functionality the NAS had.

Four multicast use cases follow. Conditional access lets the operator control access to some streams per user, to differentiate service offers or to enforce conditional access on sensitive content, though application-layer rights management may be enough in some environments. The access node can hold white, grey and black lists per access port and decide for itself: a flow on the white list is replicated straight away, one on the black list is discarded, and one on the grey list is put to the NAS, which says whether to honour it. Where a flow matches several lists the most specific match wins, and if that match is in several lists the black list beats the grey list, which beats the white list. A flow in no list at all is discarded, unless a catch-all entry changes the default.

Admission control exists because triple-play services make capacity planning hard: simply adding bandwidth is not always practical or sufficient, and the applications are delay-sensitive, loss-sensitive and non-elastic, meaning they run at a fixed bandwidth that cannot be adjusted. Before honouring a request to join a new multicast flow, the access node and the NAS together must check that there is still enough bandwidth on the access line. One arrangement has the access node query the NAS, which checks and answers. Another adds the notion of delegation of authorisation, where the NAS or policy server delegates a portion of the access-loop bandwidth to the access node, which then performs multicast admission control itself within that amount; the access node can ask for more delegated bandwidth, giving both a minimum amount that would satisfy the present request and a preferred amount that anticipates later ones, and the NAS can ask for the delegation to be reduced or released. A third has the subscriber's join and leave messages terminate on the NAS, which sets the replication state on the access node if the flow is admitted.

Accounting and reporting cover time- or volume-based accounting for particular flows on particular ports. The access node knows when replication starts and stops; it can either send that to a central accounting system itself, which is outside the scope of this document, or report it to the NAS, which generates the accounting records. The information report can be basic, saying that replication started or ended, or detailed, adding the volume replicated by including a byte count in the report sent when replication ends. The NAS tells the access node which level is needed: no reporting, basic accounting, or detailed accounting. The NAS can also query the access node asynchronously for an instantaneous status report, for troubleshooting, covering the flows on one port, the ports receiving one flow, or the flows on every port.

Spontaneous admission response lets replication be stopped on demand, for instance when prepaid credit expires, or for a content preview that lasts a fixed time. An external entity instructs the NAS to interrupt replication to a port or user, and the NAS communicates the decision to the access node with an admission response. The same message is used when the access node does not process the subscriber's IGMP messages itself, for instance because they are tunnelled, and forwards them to the NAS instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Four things the mechanism is meant to do: tell the server the real speed of a line, change a line's settings, run a test on a line, and let the cabinet copy TV streams itself rather than the server sending one copy per subscriber.

sections.title: The Requirements
sections.content:
The protocol requirements come first. ANCP must be easily extensible through new message types, must handle both ATM and Ethernet, its interactions must be reliable, and it must support request and response transactions that are atomic, so that the elements always end up in a known state whether or not the transaction succeeded. Where the NAS sends a bulk of independent decisions, the transaction applies to each decision separately rather than to the whole batch. The protocol must scale to let one NAS control at least 5000 access nodes, and its operation must be controllable from a management station, which must be able to retrieve statistics and alarms and to start operations and collect their results.

On multicast, the protocol must support providing conditional access information to access ports using the three lists, binding a list to a given access port, letting the access node query the NAS for a decision on a grey-list flow, and letting the NAS send an admission decision. Where bandwidth delegation is used, the protocol must allow the delegation, the request for more, the reduction of what was delegated and the release of what is unused. It must allow information reports when replication starts or ends and for the replicated volume, the NAS's decision on what accounting is needed, the revocation of an earlier replication decision, partial updates of the lists, and queries about what is being replicated where.

On protocol design, it should provide a shutdown sequence so the peer knows the system is going down gracefully, and a report model so the access node can send changes of state spontaneously; it should support a graceful restart so the protocol survives a network failure; and it must provide a way for the two ends to tell each other which use cases they support and to negotiate a common subset. There must be an adjacency protocol that synchronises operational state, agrees the protocol version, discovers peer identities and detects when they change, a mechanism to detect adjacency loss automatically, and the guarantee that losing the adjacency does not affect subscriber connectivity and leaves the elements in a known state. The mechanism must be independent of the underlying layer 2 technology, must use the IP protocol stack, and must use the IPoA encapsulation on ATM and the IPoE encapsulation on Ethernet.

The requirements on the access node and on the NAS follow in the same spirit, and the RFC notes that these are guidelines rather than absolute requirements, so the words must and should are not capitalised there. The access node must support at least two logical partitions, and should support eight, because one physical device may serve several wholesale providers, each with its own NAS; each access port belongs to exactly one partition, each partition has its own adjacency to a NAS and can enforce that only its own controller reaches it, and the node should be able to keep adjacencies to redundant controllers. It must process control transactions in real time, mark its messages with a high priority to avoid dropping them under congestion, report a failure to agree on capabilities to network management, raise an alarm when the adjacency is lost, use the Access Circuit Identifier format from TR-101 so that the server can correlate the messages with what it sees in DHCP and PPPoE, complete operations in the order of tens of milliseconds, and avoid bursts of messages about line attributes. Parameters such as the DSL noise margin may only be changed by the element manager, so the element manager has to configure on the access node which parameter sets may be touched through the mechanism and what defaults to use after a recovery.

The NAS must establish adjacencies only with authorised peers, run with several access nodes at once, obtain access-loop information from the access node partitions, shape traffic so as not to exceed the net data rate learned from the access node, report the attributes it has learned to a policy or AAA server using RADIUS vendor-specific attributes, and treat PPP or DHCP session state independently of the adjacency state so that subscriber sessions survive the adjacency going down. It must mark its messages as high priority, report a failure to agree capabilities, only start information exchange when there is a non-empty common set of capabilities, raise an alarm on adjacency loss, and correlate its messages with subscriber sessions using the Access Circuit Identifier. A wholesale model adds more: reporting access-loop attributes to the retail provider's gateway, a proxy architecture for L2TP wholesale so that different providers get conditional access to dedicated resources, and timely communication of generic access-line information when the NAS acts as an L2TP access concentrator.
sections.plainLanguage: The requirements fall into three piles: what the protocol itself must do, what the cabinet must do, and what the server must do. The protocol has to be reliable, transactional, extensible, and able to run over both ATM and Ethernet.

sections.title: Management-Related Requirements
sections.content:
When the mechanism is introduced, the existing management mechanisms have to keep working as before. Configuring a network element through the mechanism means that two managers can now act on the same element, the element manager and the mechanism itself, so conflicts have to be avoided. The NAS may also pass the subscriber parameters it controls to a central policy or AAA server, which can track them and apply policies, and then enforce those policies back on the NAS. For instance, where a subscriber is connected to more than one NAS, the policy server can coordinate the bandwidth available on a given access port between them.

The management-related requirements then say what must be configurable and what must be reported. The control channel transport parameters must be configurable on both the access node and the NAS, such as the VPI and VCI and the transport characteristics for ATM networks, or the C-VLAN ID, the S-VLAN ID and the p-bit marking for Ethernet networks, along with the IP address of the interface on each side. When the operational status of the control channel changes, a linkdown or linkup trap should be sent to the element management system. The access node must allow individual DSL lines to be associated with specific adjacencies using SNMP, must notify the element management system in a timely manner of configuration changes the NAS has made through the mechanism, and must allow concurrent access to the same resource from several managers, with only one manager changing anything at a time. The mechanism may also notify the NAS of configuration changes made by the element management system, but only for parameters belonging to the access-loop configuration use case.
sections.plainLanguage: The mechanism has to fit alongside the existing management systems rather than replace them, so the two must not fight over the same settings, and both sides need ways to check what the other has changed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 5713 lists the ANCP-related security threats that could be encountered on the access node and the NAS, develops a threat model and identifies the security requirements for ANCP, aiming to decide which security functions are needed at the protocol level. The protocol must comply with those requirements, and the access node must not allow Access Node Control messages to be sent towards the customer premises.

The multicast handling described here adds one risk. ANCP activity between the access node and the NAS is triggered by join and leave requests from the end-user equipment, and that could be used for denial-of-service attacks against the access node or the NAS. The RFC notes this is not a new class of risk, because subscribers can already send IGMP messages to the NAS when the access node does no IGMP snooping, and the risk is transparent as long as the processing of ANCP messages on the NAS and the access node is comparably efficient and protected against congestion. To mitigate it, the access node may implement control-plane protection such as limiting how many multicast flows a user can join at once or limiting the rate of joins and leaves from a given user. The RFC also observes that an operator can easily protect against attacks using invalid multicast flows by using the mask-based match in the black list, so that joins for invalid flows are denied at the access node with no ANCP interaction and no involvement of the NAS.
sections.plainLanguage: The security requirements themselves are set out in a separate RFC. This one adds that the video channel joins must not become a way to flood the cabinet, and that invalid streams can be blocked locally without asking the server.
